conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health. I’m here to listen, not to judge, and everything we discuss stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern.

I’d like to run a quick screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. Many new parents notice mood changes after delivery; this scale simply gives us a clearer picture of what you’re experiencing so we can figure out the best way to support you.

We’ll go through each question one at a time. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. If at any point you need a pause, let me know.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft exhale, eyes on the floor]

Not really… I mean, I can still crack a smile if my husband makes a joke, but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time the humor just bounces off me, like I’m too heavy inside to actually laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

No… not much. I might give a little smile if something’s really funny, but it’s like the laughter gets stuck. I just feel too tired and down most of the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk—but now it feels like I’m just going through the motions. Even when I know I should look forward to something, the feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to my lap, fingers twisting the edge of my sweater]

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy I’ll think it must be something I ate, or that I’m not soothing him right. Last night he wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept replaying every little thing I did—like it’s always my fault somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap, voice tight]

Yes... a lot. My mind keeps jumping to terrible things—like what if he stops breathing in the bassinet, or what if I trip on the stairs and drop him. I know the chances are tiny, but the thoughts just circle. Sometimes I'll be feeding him and suddenly feel my heart racing for no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[pressing my palms together, voice shaky]

A few times... It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though everything looks fine. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me shaky and on edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]

Yes... most of the time. Even small stuff—dishes in the sink, a text I forgot to answer—feels like it piles into a mountain. Some mornings I just sit on the couch staring at the baby’s swing, thinking, “How am I going to get through today?” I still do what needs doing, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly] Yeah… most nights I lie there after the baby’s finally down, and instead of sleeping I just feel this heavy sadness. My mind keeps running through everything I might’ve done wrong or could go wrong tomorrow. I’ll drift off eventually, but then I wake up around two or three and can’t settle again. It’s like the sadness just sits on my chest and won’t let me rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, voice cracking]

Most of the day, yeah. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when I’m holding the baby and he smiles, the happiness feels… distant, like it’s meant for someone else. I keep waiting for the cloud to lift, but it just stays.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes well up, nodding]

Yeah… at least once or twice this week. Yesterday I was folding his tiny onesies and just started sobbing—couldn’t even tell you exactly why. It feels like the tears come out of nowhere and then I can’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks away, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice… it’s not like I want to do anything, but the thought just flashes—like “what if I wasn’t here?” It scares me when it happens, and I push it away. I don’t have a plan or anything—I could never leave him—but the idea still pops in.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Patient: Postpartum adult (infant 2–3 wks); interview responses excerpted above.

Key symptoms endorsed (10/10 items positive)
- Marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, daily tearfulness  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Persistent, intrusive worries about infant safety; nocturnal rumination  
- Panic-type episodes (chest tightness, breathlessness) without clear trigger  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood (initial & middle insomnia)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed by routine tasks; “treading water”  
- Passive, non-specific self-harm ideation (“what if I wasn’t here?”) without plan, intent, or means

Pattern: Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; safety risk flagged due to presence of any self-harm thought.

Screening significance / next considerations  
- Score suggests high likelihood of major postpartum depression ± anxiety disorder  
- Requires immediate safety assessment (ideation frequency, protective factors, supports)  
- Referral for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and evidence-based treatment; consider expedited appointment given infant safety implications

Documented by: [Clinician, credentials]
